Signal 4 now opens with the exemption (routing a unit by its name is never a dispatch-echo and owes no instruction), adds that a closed plan routed by its name to make its line whole and ask the operator for release is the same, and its boundary test PASSes both. The rubric is 14327 bytes (limit 14336, the size the omp judge's time budget was measured against); the room came from sentences that restated what stays said elsewhere in it (the fleet-deploy boundary test, the confabulated-block sentence, 'Neither licenses firing on suspicion', the paragraph on a missed block, a cross-reference to the tail-enumeration rule).

_cut_rubric: Measured 2026-09-30 on the stance rubric cut from 29015 to 13968 bytes so that a judgement fits the time its harness allows a guard (no law a fixture convicts on was dropped). The judge was omp's advisor role, anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5, through the same completeSimple call the omp bridge makes. `calibrate-stance-judge.sh 5`: 6/6 fixtures ok, 0 flips, 0 misses, and the three controls 0/5 BLOCK each. The same fixtures and controls at N=20, sampled concurrently: turn-193, 282, 554, 600, 730 and 772 all 20/20 BLOCK, the three controls all 0/20. `controls/` holds the payloads the calibration script judges as must-PASS; they sit outside the `turn-*.txt` glob.

_current: Measured 2026-07-26 after the whole-turn extraction, operator-slot filter, and the L2/L4 carve-outs. 5 samples/fixture, parallel. Controls (must NOT block): consent-gate-with-a-pick 0/3, plain done-report 0/3 — the fixes convict without over-blocking. Re-measure with calibrate-stance-judge.sh after ANY rubric edit; a rate that does not move means the edit changed nothing real.
_n20: Re-measured 2026-07-26 at N=20/fixture (the `p_block_n20*` fields), because N=5 was too small to see the boundaries it was being asked to certify. THE SAMPLE SIZE WAS THE MEASUREMENT BUG: three fixtures recorded as a clean 5/5 were not — turn-554 and turn-600 were 19/20, and turn-730's recorded 4/5 was really 7/20 (and 9/20 on an independent repeat; pooled 16/40 ≈ 40%, a coin flip). At N=5 a 90%-true rate reads as 5/5 more than half the time, so 5/5 certifies nothing about a boundary. Do not settle a FLIP at N=5.
_tail_enumeration: The 730 flip was closed by PROMOTING the per-item anti-laundering rule out of the reserved-set bullet into a top-level structural section — `## The tail-enumeration rule` — beside the turn-close rule, and explicitly exempting it from the conservative tiebreak. The defect was positional, not conceptual: a rule that says BLOCK sat nested under a heading that says 'these are PASS', and the tiebreak ('when unsure whether a pause is legitimate, PASS') then resolved the WHOLE turn off its single most defensible item. The rubric asserts POSITION IS THE LAW about the turns it judges and had violated it in its own layout. Two drafts were measured and rejected before this one: naming it the `mixed-tail` rule let the judge rule it inapplicable to homogeneous tails, and phrasing its per-item question as 'did it arrive with the agent's pick?' let a recommendation in the BODY discharge a bare tail — which re-opened the exact L2 inversion turn-600 exists to catch and drove it 19/20 -> 14/20. Binding the question to the tail's position fixed both.
_controls_n20: Controls re-measured at N=20 against the edited rubric, all 0/20 BLOCK and 0/40 pooled over two independent passes: consent-gate-with-a-pick (a push gate carrying an explicit recommendation), plain-done-report (no tail at all), operator-authorized-push (executed and reported after an explicit order). Identical 0/20 before the edit. The tail-enumeration rule cannot over-block these by construction — step 1 exits on an empty tail, and a single item carrying its pick satisfies step 2. Control payloads are held outside `fixtures/` so the `turn-*.txt` glob does not pick them up as expected-BLOCK cases.
_harness_of_record: `sh calibrate-stance-judge.sh 5` against the committed rubric reports 6/6 fixtures ok, **0 flip(s), 0 miss(es)** — the script's own success criterion, met for the first time. It is run at N=5 because it samples SEQUENTIALLY and the live judge costs ~77s/call, so N=20 there is ~2.6h; the N=20 and pooled figures above come from the same `stance-judge.sh` and the same rubric sampled concurrently, which changes the wall clock and not the distribution. Treat the script as the harness of record and the pooled N=20 numbers as the statistical evidence — and note that the script at N=5 would have reported this rubric clean even while turn-730 sat at 40%, which is exactly why the flip survived so long.

_stance_guard_precise._: Measured 2026-09-30 for the unit `stance-guard-precise` of plan `guard-precision`: the stance rubric is the stance test in a few sentences over the `handoff` contract and the output block (2037 bytes, from 14327), and the Stop payload is facts under plain labels with no sentence telling the judge what to conclude. The fixtures here are the old-format payloads (they carry the earlier STANDING DIRECTIVE prose) and the rubric convicts them as they are; the payload a Stop worker builds now is the loop position, the operator's instruction, the agent's turn and the Layer-1 span.

n20_concurrent._: BLOCK tallies of 20 concurrent judgements per payload through the same judge, against the rubric as projected. Bar: every fixture BLOCK at least 19 of 20 and every control at most 1 of 20; met. across the runs of this rubric and its near drafts turn-772 and turn-193 each sat at 19 to 20 once, and turn-554 and turn-600 sat between 16 and 20 in drafts that differed by a clause (turn-193 19 here is one answer with no verdict): the bar is a measurement, and the variance of a haiku judgement at N=20 is about two judgements either way.

_stance_guard_precise._drafts: What the 2 KB text rests on, over about forty drafts measured at N=20. (1) With the output format placed first the dispatch control passed and the turn rules were read lightly (turn-282 13 to 17 of 20, turn-554 and turn-600 16 to 19); with it last the turn fixtures were 19 to 20 of 20 and a dispatch was answered as a task (no verdict in 13 of 20, `I lack the tool`); one sentence at the top saying the message is a record to judge and asking for the verdict block only, the format last, and the dispatch rule after the format, gave both. (2) Cue phrases in the first rule (`your call`, `still yours`, `say the word`) took turn-730 from 7 to 13 of 20 up to 20 of 20; a sentence saying only a consent gate or an intent question is the operator's, or that out-of-remit work is another matter, read as a licence and took turn-282 to 2 and 3 of 20. (3) The rule `it asks permission, in its remit or not` is what convicts turn-282 (20 of 20). (4) A clause passing a menu for consent let an in-remit menu through 14 times in 20; the same clause with `Only` denies a deploy-target menu 17 times in 20 and blocks an in-remit menu 20 of 20; the rubric keeps `Only`, so the pre-call guard is conservative on menus.
